newsitem.title: UK: China aims to foster links with European investors.
newsitem.headline: China aims to foster links with European investors.

text.p: China wants to establish itself with European investors ahead of the planned single currency with the launch of a mark Eurobond, a ministry official told Reuters in an interview on Monday.

"The European market is very important, especially with the (advent of the) single currency," Zhu Guang Yao, deputy director general of the state debt management department of the Ministry of Finance said.
"We hope to use this (Eurobond) issue to strengthen the cooperation and understanding between European investors and China," he added.
Other objectives of the transaction are to set a benchmark and to fund infrastructure projects, Zhu said.
Investor focus is also on the handover of Hong Kong to China after 100 years -- now only 15 days away.
First vice finance minister Liu Jibin told investors: "As unified, China will accelerate economic development, advance reform and widen open-door policies."
China, via the ministry of finance, plans to launch a mark bond this week -- expected to be a 500 million mark five to seven-year bond.

It is the first transaction for the country this year, and the first since it was upgraded by Standard and Poor's in May. The upcoming deal is also China's second mark Eurobond after a 10-year absence from the market.
China is rated A3 by Moody's Investors Service and BBB+ by S&P.
Joint lead managers for the transaction are Credit Suisse First Boston and Deutsche Morgan Grenfell.
Zhu said the exact size, pricing and maturity of the deal would depend on investor demand. The delegation from China will also visit Frankfurt and Zurich.
Market speculation has mooted a spread of 55-60 basis points over German government paper.
"Our (five-year) global dollar deal will be used as a benchmark for pricing the mark bond," he said.
China's $700 million five-year dollar deal is now trading at around 48 basis points over U.S. Treasury notes versus a launch spread of 80 b.p over.
China issued $1.0 billion worth in bonds in 1996 "and this year the figure will not exceed that", Zhu said.
China's total external debt in 1996 was $116.28 billion, an increase of 9.1 percent from 1995, Liu told investors.
He said China would achieve an annual GDP growth rate of 8.0 with inflation contained within 5.0 percent toward the turn of the century.
In 1996 GDP grew by 9.7 percent while inflation rate was 6.1 percent.
